tagline: Ocean beaches, forest valleys and lake shores along the Olympic loop
intro: Washington’s Pacific Coast Scenic Byway follows US 101 along ocean beaches and through rain forests, circling the Olympic Peninsula. State of Washington Tourism promotes the route for its beaches, mountains, maritime history and seafood, and recommends five days for its Olympia-to-Long Beach itinerary. The drive includes a pair of hairpin turns north of the Hoh River and a close passage along Lake Crescent’s southern shore.

US 101 received its number in 1926, incorporating two earlier state roads. Construction of the Olympic Loop Highway’s final section began the following year. It opened in August 1931 with a two-day dedication. The road provides access to Olympic National Park by spur roads; no road crosses the Olympic Mountains.

From the Columbia River, cross the Astoria-Megler Bridge and follow US 101 through Ilwaco and along Willapa Bay to Raymond and Aberdeen. Beyond Lake Quinault, the road reaches the Pacific near Kalaloch, turns inland at Ruby Beach and continues through Forks. Lake Crescent leads into the northern stretch toward Port Angeles and Sequim. The highway then turns south at Discovery Bay and follows Hood Canal through Brinnon and Hoodsport, passing Shelton on the way to Olympia and its end at I-5 in Tumwater.

moments.title: Ruby Beach
moments.text: Ruby-like crystals in the sand gave Ruby Beach its name. Driftwood and sea stacks mark the beach, the northernmost of Olympic National Park’s southern coastal beaches. It lies on Highway 101 in Jefferson County, 27 miles south of Forks. Here the highway turns northeast and follows the Hoh River inland. Destruction Island and its lighthouse are visible about four miles offshore to the southwest. These coastal waters and offshore islands are protected by three national wildlife refuges and the Olympic Coast National Marine Sanctuary.

moments.title: Forks
moments.text: Forks’ timber history has a mechanical landmark in Tillicum Park: Rayonier No. 10, a Shay locomotive retired there in 1959. Lima built No. 10 in 1930; Rayonier acquired it in 1945 for its logging operation near Forks. Shay engines used a crankshaft along the side to power all their wheels, a design used to haul lumber from forests. Timber harvesting remains part of the local economy, below its 1970s peak. Another chapter arrived when Stephenie Meyer chose Forks for Twilight after searching Google for rainy settings. The town now has a Forever Twilight in Forks Collection alongside its logging history.

moments.title: Lake Crescent
moments.text: US 101 stays close to Lake Crescent’s southern shore, while a former logging railway follows the lake’s north side. The Spruce Railroad Trail occupies that old railway grade, including an old railroad tunnel. The lake fills a valley carved by glaciers during the last Ice Age. Low nitrogen levels limit algae growth, helping give the water its clarity and blue color. The lake became part of the Olympic Forest Reserve in 1897, a recreation area in 1921 and part of Olympic National Park in 1938. Its water leaves by the Lyre River, passes over Lyre River Falls and reaches the Strait of Juan de Fuca.
